## Summary {.unlisted}
This website offers the concepts, examples and practical resources needed to get started with RCTs, both for those considering one for the first time and for those who already have experience with experimentation.
This page explains what RCTs are, how RCTs fit among other impact evaluation methods, which questions they can answer, and why they matter for cohesion policy. It ends with a guide to the rest of the site.
:::

## What is an RCT?
Experimentation, or experimental evaluation, means testing an intervention by assigning eligible participants at random either to receive it (or one version of it) or to a comparison group (also called a control group) that does not receive it, or receives a different version. This is called a randomised controlled trial (RCT). On this website, the words experimentation and RCTs are used interchangeably.
Randomisation can be used, for example, when there are more eligible applicants than available places, or when an intervention is rolled out in phases and the order in which participants receive it is decided at random. Comparing average outcomes between the groups shows whether the intervention - and not something else going on at the same time - is the reason for the observed changes.
Who ends up in which group is decided by a random draw. It is not decided by who applied first, who looked most promising, or whom the reviewer favoured. Because assignment is random, the groups are similar on average before the intervention starts, and any remaining differences between them are due only to chance. That is true not just for characteristics that can be measured, but also for those that cannot be observed. So when a difference between the groups shows up later, it can be attributed to the intervention, provided the trial is implemented as planned and outcomes are measured in the same way for both groups.

## What is impact evaluation - and where do RCTs fit in?

::: {.gold-panel}
Impact evaluation answers the question: what causal effect did this intervention have
on outcomes like employment, skills or firm growth - for whom did it work
best, and under which conditions?
:::

An impact evaluation compares what happened after an intervention was introduced with what
would have happened in its absence: the counterfactual. Unlike monitoring, which tracks whether an intervention is implemented as planned, it tests
whether the intervention caused a real difference. It is one of several types of evaluation, alongside implementation evaluation, that managing authorities can include in their evaluation plans. See [what impact evaluation is for and
how it differs from M&E](01-why-and-when.qmd#impact-evaluation).

There is more than one credible way to conduct an impact evaluation, and the right choice depends on the intervention, the available data and the timing.
Quasi-experimental methods such as matching,
difference-in-differences, or regression discontinuity design, compare participants to similar
non-participants constructing the comparison group after the intervention had already ended. That is impact
evaluation too, and it can be credible. Because the evaluator does not decide who ends up in which group, the comparability of the groups rests on assumptions that need to be stated and discussed. 

Now imagine doing this differently: designing the comparison group by randomly assigning eligible applicants to different groups, rather than picking it afterwards. That is what an RCT does.
See below [how the methods compare](01-why-and-when.qmd#alternatives) and [why RCTs are usually the stronger
choice](01-why-and-when.qmd#rct).

## Why introduce experimental evaluations?

Innovation in policymaking to maximise returns on European cohesion policy investments is crucial for improving Europe’s competitiveness. Innovation is particularly vital for middle-income countries to avoid the middle-income trap by integrating advanced technologies and enhancing productivity. Innovation also drives the efficient use of capital, labour, and energy. This is essential for sustainable development - especially in light of rising debt, ageing populations, and environmental challenges.

The European Union (EU) is one of the world’s largest investors in innovation. Research and innovation received roughly a tenth of its €361 billion cohesion policy budget for 2021-2027. Yet regional disparities in innovation outcomes persist and limit the EU’s competitiveness.

To keep pace with global competitors, every euro invested needs to yield greater returns. While innovation is a primary goal, the process to achieve it often lacks mechanisms for continuous learning and improvement.

Successful policy development must be accompanied by ongoing adaptation to evolving circumstances.

::: {.gold-panel}
This is called science-based adaptive delivery: testing, learning, and
adjusting as you go.
:::

Concretely, getting more out of cohesion policy investments means rethinking how to identify the beneficiaries who benefit most from public support. How can one know whether funded beneficiaries would have performed just as well without public funding? Or would other recipients have benefited more and generated even greater returns on public investments? Experimentation can help answer these questions.

### Hear from European Commission representatives on why experimentation matters
::: {.video-frame}
{{< video https://youtu.be/p9L2-K7UyP0 title="The case for policy learning and experimentation" aspect-ratio="16x9" >}}
:::


## RCTs show what works and how effectively

An RCT compares what happens to intervention participants against an on-average identical group that does not receive the intervention. That comparison can show whether the cohesion policy intervention - and not something else going on at the same time - is the reason for the observed changes.

Who ends up in the treatment group (receiving the intervention) and who ends up in the comparison group (receiving no intervention, or a different type of intervention) is decided by a random draw. It is not decided by who applied first, who looked most promising, or whom the reviewer favoured. Because assignment to the intervention is random, the two groups have the same characteristics on average before the intervention. That is true not just for characteristics you can measure, but also for the ones you
cannot observe. So when a difference between the groups shows up later, it can be attributed to the intervention.

An RCT can answer several kinds of questions, depending on how it is designed:

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
### How effective is a given intervention? {.unlisted}
Whether the intervention works, and for whom it works best.
:::
::: {.card-e}
### Which version of an intervention is most effective? {.unlisted}
How different versions of an intervention compare - which parts of an intervention work, which do not, and
how they work together.
:::
::: {.card-e}
### How should an intervention be delivered? {.unlisted}
How different delivery mechanisms change results, including how to target beneficiaries
accurately and increase take-up.
:::
::: {.card-e}
### Is it worth the cost? {.unlisted}
How cost-effective the intervention is, and how it compares to other interventions.
:::
:::
The question one wants answered decides when, how, and for whom the RCT has to be planned. To find out whether
an intervention works at all, randomisation must be built in before launch, from the call for
proposals. To find out which version works better (a grant alone versus a grant plus
advisory support, for instance), an RCT can still be added after the intervention has started.
Randomisation then shifts from who gets funded at all to which version each participant
receives. See below [Choosing the right evaluation design](01-why-and-when.qmd#choosing-design).

:::

### Do you think you already know which intervention works and whom to fund? {.statement .unlisted}

Every euro you commit is a euro you cannot spend elsewhere. To ensure resources are spent efficiently, ask yourself:

- Would the beneficiaries have succeeded without your agency's support?

- Would someone else have gained more from the same euro?

If you cannot answer both with confidence, consider testing it. [See why funding the
strongest applicants may be less impactful than funding marginal
ones](01-why-and-when.qmd#allocation).


### Common myths about RCTs
:::: {.myths-grid}

<details class="myth-box">
<summary>RCTs are too scientific for anyone but academics</summary>

RCTs are the easiest rigorous evaluation method to interpret and implement, not the hardest. Randomisation is, at its core, just like flipping a coin: who lands in the treatment and who lands in the comparison group is solely a matter of chance and unrelated to any characteristics of the applicant. This ensures that the treatment and comparison groups are, on average, identical in the absence of the intervention. Because of this, the impact estimate does not rest on assumptions that have to be separately defended - it is simply the difference in average outcomes between the two groups after the intervention runs.

Quasi-experimental methods - e.g. difference-in-differences, matching, regression discontinuity - can seem less academic because they do not need to be embedded at the design stage; they work with what is already there. But the estimates they produce rely on assumptions that are hard to verify. Properly checking whether their key assumption holds - that trends really were parallel, that matched groups did not differ on anything unobserved, that the cut-off was clean - requires robustness checks beyond a standard regression. An RCT needs none of that: if assignment was random, the treatment and comparison groups are comparable by construction, and the average difference between them is the estimate.

So RCTs may look more academic but are, in practice, more transparent and easier to defend. They are also straightforward to implement and not necessarily more costly to run (see below).

</details>

<details class="myth-box">
<summary>Random assignment is not allowed under European rules and contradicts the principle of selecting on merit</summary>

Random assignment is not only allowed but is, in many cases, the fairer way to select. The Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy (DG REGIO) has formally confirmed that randomisation is permissible under EU cohesion policy rules (for more information, see [A legal basis for random selection](02.03c-legal.qmd)).

Random assignment does not replace selection on merit but can supplement it. To illustrate this, imagine a two-stage process in which all applicants are first assessed against the call's eligibility and quality criteria as usual. In the second stage, only those who pass enter the draw. Expert panels still decide who is eligible, but they do not rank or choose among equally eligible applicants. Interventions can also be designed to fund the strongest applicants outright and randomise only within a middle band of scores, as was done in [Extremadura](03-examples.qmd#spain).

Randomisation is already used to select intervention beneficiaries across Europe. managing authorities and agencies in Spain, Czechia, Croatia and Romania have used random assignment to allocate EU-funded support, as has the European Commission itself for SME energy-efficiency grants across 34 countries, and interventions in Bulgaria and Poland are preparing to do the same (see [Examples](03-examples.qmd)). The use of randomisation is not limited to cohesion policy. In France, where policy experimentation has had a constitutional basis since 2003, the Ministry of Labour randomised intensive job counselling for young graduates across 235 local labour markets, with nearly 30,000 job seekers in the evaluation sample [(Crépon et al., 2013)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjt001). In Spain, the Inclusion Policy Lab of the Ministry of Inclusion, Social Security and Migration has funded 32 randomised evaluations of social inclusion interventions linked to the national minimum income scheme.

</details>

<details class="myth-box">
<summary>RCTs are the gold standard for evaluation</summary>

For establishing whether an intervention caused a change in outcomes, RCTs are the gold standard. Their design minimises bias and establishes clear cause-and-effect relationships because the estimate does not depend on an assumption that has to be separately defended: no parallel trends to argue for, no unobserved characteristics to control for, no instrument to justify. Every other rigorous method earns its credibility by convincingly defending an assumption that cannot be directly tested, while a well-designed and executed RCT does not need to make that argument.

</details>

<details class="myth-box">
<summary>RCTs are more expensive than other rigorous methods</summary>

Randomisation is an allocation rule. It tells you who is assigned to an intervention and who is not, but says nothing about how you measure outcomes afterwards. Measuring outcomes (for example, profits, business survival) requires data, which costs money and takes time - not just for RCTs but for whichever evaluation method is used. Other rigorous methods often skip a baseline survey, which RCTs generally plan from design stage. That may look like a saving at first glance, but it makes it harder to assess the credibility of the assumptions those methods rely on. With a large enough sample, RCTs technically do not need a baseline survey either, though collecting one is best practice. Where outcomes are already recorded in administrative registers, the cost of an RCT is the same as that of any other rigorous evaluation: legal/GDPR clearance to access and link the registers, and analytical time.

RCTs do come with additional staffing costs. Unlike a method applied retrospectively to data that already exists, randomisation must be run and monitored while the intervention is ongoing - so the managing authority needs staff assigned to it on an ongoing basis.

</details>

<details class="myth-box">
<summary>RCTs tell you an intervention works but never why</summary>

If well-designed, RCTs are among the strongest tools available for showing why an intervention works. When an intervention has several components, a multi-arm design lets you disentangle their separate contributions: instead of one treatment group and one comparison group, you randomise across several treatment arms that receive different components or combinations of components (for example, a grant alone versus a grant combined with business advisory support) and compare outcomes across arms rather than against a single comparison group.

</details>

<details class="myth-box">
<summary>You can only identify what you randomised</summary>

This is true, which is why it matters to get the learning questions you care about right at the design stage. Randomisation gives a clean estimate of the effect of whatever was randomised - most commonly, being assigned to (or offered) an intervention. To cleanly separate the effect of one component from another, those components need to be randomised separately too, for example through a multi-arm design.

</details>

<details class="myth-box">
<summary>RCTs are only valid inside the study population</summary>

Every empirical method faces the same question of whether findings hold up beyond the sample they were estimated on, so external validity is not a defect unique to randomisation. A single RCT cannot tell you whether an intervention will work everywhere, but it can tell you a lot about the conditions under which it worked in that case. When designing a new intervention elsewhere, you can assess how similar those conditions are and judge how far the original findings are likely to apply. The more similar RCTs are run across different countries or regions, the more confidently general conclusions can be drawn.

</details>

<details class="myth-box">
<summary>RCTs take too long to be useful within a programming period</summary>

A staggered or phased rollout combined with an RCT can be a source of continuous learning. Early waves of participants already generate short-term outcomes while later waves are still being enrolled, so a managing authority can see early signals - take-up, engagement, first movements in outcomes - well before the intervention is fully rolled out, and adjust design or targeting for later waves accordingly. Long-term outcomes can, by construction, only be observed after a few years, which may come too late to change the current programming period. But similar interventions are likely to follow, in the same region or elsewhere in the EU, so knowing whether an intervention achieved its intended effect still helps allocate future funding more efficiently.

</details>

<details class="myth-box">
<summary>RCTs assume everyone responds the same way</summary>

The effects an RCT most commonly measures - the average treatment effect, or the intention-to-treat effect - compare average outcomes between the treatment and comparison groups. Neither assumes every member of these groups responds identically, only that the average difference is a meaningful summary of the intervention's impact. Heterogeneous treatment effect analysis by subgroup is feasible with a large enough sample and cheap to do well with EU administrative data: business and tax registers already record the characteristics on which one may suspect heterogeneity (for example, firm size, sector, region) needed to check whether an intervention works differently for different types of firms.

</details>

<details class="myth-box">
<summary>Randomisation means no further analysis is needed</summary>

If sample sizes are large enough and treatment is assigned randomly, the treatment and comparison groups will show, on average, identical characteristics - not that every participant has an identical match in the other group, only that characteristics balance on average. In practice, participants do not always stay in the group they were originally assigned to. This happens when randomisation is on assignment to an intervention rather than on take-up: the assigned and non-assigned groups still look the same, but the group that actually participates no longer looks the same as those who do not. In this case, what is reported is the intention-to-treat effect - the average effect of being assigned to the intervention, rather than of participating in it. Good practice is to check balance between the treatment and comparison groups on observable characteristics at baseline, before the intervention starts.

</details>

<details class="myth-box">
<summary>RCTs can only be run on a big sample</summary>

Detecting a given effect with confidence needs enough observations in each group - the smaller the expected effect, the bigger the sample must be. This is why one should conduct power calculations at the design stage.

A power calculation needs a few inputs: the smallest effect that would still be meaningful to detect, how much the outcome already varies across firms before the intervention runs, expectations about intervention take-up (as this affects the treatment group's sample size), how much observation loss to expect over time, and whether assignment happens at the level of the applicant or of a group they belong to - assigning by group rather than by firm generally needs a larger total sample to reach the same precision.

See [How to conduct an RCT](02-how.qmd) for a walkthrough of turning these inputs into an actual sample size calculation.

</details>

<details class="myth-box">
<summary>It is difficult to get responses from the comparison group</summary>

This concern is valid and worth considering at design stage, but it is often a smaller challenge than expected. Often, outcomes of interest are already captured in administrative registers rather than collected through a survey, so comparison group response rates are not a concern at all.

If outcome data needs to be collected through surveys, a group that received nothing may feel less invested in answering than a group that participated. But the evidence suggests the gap is usually smaller than expected: looking across dozens of studies, David McKenzie found that differential attrition between treatment and comparison groups averages only a few percentage points, widening mainly when the treatment is large and highly visible (for example, a sizeable cash grant) rather than for lower-value interventions. Where a gap does open up in an early round, sustained follow-up - repeat calls, alternative contact channels, incentives - has been shown to close much of it later.

</details>

<details class="myth-box">
<summary>RCTs are unethical because they deny help to a comparison group</summary>

This common misconception gets the ethics backwards. Where limited budgets already mean fewer applicants can be funded than apply, someone is turned away regardless of the evaluation method - the budget already decides that. Randomisation only decides how the budget is allocated. Executed well, it is a well-documented, defensible allocation rule that gives every equally eligible applicant the same fair chance to access funds. Other ways of assigning applicants - case-officer discretion, queue position - are no fairer, less transparent, and not necessarily more accurate. If there is empirical, causal evidence that a particular group of applicants should be prioritised, that evidence should be used; if there is not, these alternatives are no fairer than random assignment. In a business plan competition in Nigeria, for instance, expert judges' scores had no relationship with which businesses went on to survive, hire staff, or turn a profit three years later, and machine-learning models trained on the same applications did barely better [(McKenzie & Sansone, 2019)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jdeveco.2019.07.002).

Nor does a comparison group have to mean receiving nothing at all: RCTs can compare two different versions of an intervention, so every participant receives some form of support and the question becomes which version works better. What matters is that participants are properly informed about the study, their rights, and how any data on them is processed and stored - which is why RCTs are typically reviewed beforehand by a research ethics committee (an Institutional Review Board, or IRB, in some countries), which is also the body participants can turn to with complaints.

</details>

<details class="myth-box">
<summary>RCTs require ethical clearance</summary>

Whether ethics review is legally mandatory depends on the country, the institution running the study, the type of intervention, and whether personal data is involved - it is not a universal legal requirement. For example, an RCT studying an intervention's effect on firms using administrative data as outcomes does not require ethical clearance. Seeking one anyway is still recommended: a research ethics committee (an Institutional Review Board) is what ensures participants are properly informed, that data handling complies with GDPR, and that there is a body participants can turn to with complaints.

</details>
